summary:
Floods are among the deadliest disasters in Türkiye, yet they are often overshadowed by earthquakes. Since 2010, 1,424 floods in Türkiye have claimed 251 lives and submerged more than 163,000 hectares. Steep terrain, heavy rainfall, construction on floodplains and inadequate drainage turn extreme rain into catastrophe.

TIFD is a web platform that connects satellite observations to their impact on people. At its core is the TIFD Raindrop Simulation, which solves the shallow water equations used by real flood models on Türkiye’s actual terrain. It shows, hour by hour, where rain flows and where it collects. Where data is available, initial soil moisture comes from NASA–ISRO NISAR measurements. Water depth and velocity are combined into a map of danger to people, and the deepest points are marked. We demonstrate the model on the 2021 Bozkurt flood, and anyone can try it by scanning a QR code.

We chose NISAR because its radar sees through clouds, day and night, exactly when optical satellites fail during storms. Our Marmara Lake case study shows how repeated satellite observations can reveal changes in water surface. Our next step is to combine NISAR flood-extent data with urban maps and verified disaster records, so communities can identify flood-prone areas and protect their homes, farmland and lives.
details:
What does it do?

TIFD (Turkish International Flood Detector) is a bilingual (English/Turkish) web platform, Hydro-SAR Türkiye, that helps people understand where floods happen in Türkiye, why they happen, and what happens when water reaches people’s lives. It has three parts:

Flood education hub: explains how a flood forms (rain saturated ground runoff and overflow) and the four flood types that affect Türkiye: flash, river, urban and coastal. For each type it gives the cause, typical warning time and real Turkish examples, such as the 2021 Western Black Sea (Bozkurt) flood. A live ticker shows ongoing floods around the world.

TIFD Raindrop Simulation: an interactive flood model running on Türkiye’s real terrain.

Surface water change explorer: a Marmara Lake case study showing how satellite data reveals the lake’s shrinking water surface over the years.

How does it work?

The simulation covers a 20 × 20 km region (demonstrated on Bozkurt, Kastamonu) on a 200 × 200 grid. In physical mode it solves the shallow water equations, the same equations used by operational flood models, and advances them hour by hour to show where rain flows and where it collects. A simpler raindrop mode is also available for quick, intuitive exploration. Users choose the rainfall intensity (light, heavy, extreme).

Where data is available, the model takes initial soil moisture from NASA–ISRO NISAR measurements, because wet soil absorbs less water and produces more runoff. Users can also overlay a NISAR radar scene on the map. At each cell, water depth and velocity are combined into a hazard-to-people index, and the deepest points are highlighted.

The Marmara Lake explorer uses the JRC Global Surface Water dataset (30 m, 2010–2021) with a year slider to visualize long-term change in surface water.

Why NISAR?

Floods happen under storm clouds, exactly when optical satellites are blind. NISAR’s L-band radar sees through clouds day and night, and its frequent repeat observations make it possible to detect changes in water coverage and soil moisture.

What benefits does it have?

It shows people and local authorities which areas are flood-prone, so they can protect homes, farmland and lives.

It shows the link between flood damage and human decisions such as construction on floodplains and poor drainage.

It makes flood physics understandable for non-experts: anyone can scan the QR code and run the simulation.

What do we hope to achieve?

We want floods to get the attention in Türkiye that earthquakes already do. Next, we plan to combine NISAR-derived flood extents with urban maps and verified disaster records, extend the simulation to more high-risk regions, and validate it against observed events like Bozkurt 2021.
